intros.market: Five CAs control 88% of issuance volume, led by Internet Security Research Group (32%), Google Trust Services (21%), and DigiCert (18%). The three-firm concentration ratio stands at 71%, with an HHI of 1980 indicating moderate concentration. This market structure creates systemic dependency on a small number of operators, while 74 tail CAs collectively serve the remaining 12% of the ecosystem.
intros.trust: 335 roots are distributed across four trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four programs and just 38 CA owners achieve universal inclusion. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating significant store disagreement that forces CAs to manage multiple chain-building strategies. This fragmentation means a certificate chain trusted in Edge may fail validation in Chrome or Safari, imposing operational complexity on both CAs and relying parties.
intros.conc: The top three CAs issue 71% of all certificates, yielding an HHI of 1980 that signals moderate market concentration with systemic risk. Internet Security Research Group alone accounts for nearly one-third of the global certificate supply. A compliance failure or operational incident at any of these top-tier providers would immediately affect hundreds of millions of TLS connections, while the 74 tail CAs collectively represent only 12% of issuance.
intros.tail: 74 CAs each issue less than 1% of global certificate volume yet hold full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk exposure for browsers and relying parties. These low-volume operators face the same compliance obligations and audit requirements as high-volume providers, but operational incidents receive less public scrutiny and their governance often lacks the resources of larger competitors. The tail's collective 12% market share means browsers must monitor and enforce policy across dozens of small operators to protect the same user base served by three large CAs.
intros.geo: US-incorporated CAs issue 93% of all certificates, with 15 operators headquartered in the United States dominating global issuance. Europe hosts 44 CAs but accounts for only 7% of volume, while 17 Asia-Pacific CAs collectively issue 0.09% despite serving billions of users in their home regions. This geographic concentration in US jurisdiction creates both operational efficiency and jurisdictional dependency, as the vast majority of certificate issuance flows through entities subject to US legal frameworks and government authority.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion but issue only 0.09% of global certificate volume. These entities span multiple jurisdictions including high-risk regions identified in the jurisdiction analysis, raising questions about state surveillance capabilities and compelled cooperation. Despite low issuance volume, their presence in root programs grants governments the technical capability to intercept TLS traffic for any domain, whether or not they currently exercise that authority at scale.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk for compelled disclosure or surveillance, including China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong, with India and Turkey designated moderate-risk. CAs incorporated in these regions face legal frameworks that may compel cooperation with state intelligence agencies, certificate issuance for surveillance purposes, or disclosure of private keys. Combined with the 93% US concentration in the geography analysis, the WebPKI exhibits acute jurisdictional concentration that exposes the ecosystem to coordinated legal pressure from a small number of nation-states.
intros.ops: 1,743 incidents across 55 CAs have been recorded, with misissuance (671 incidents) and governance failures (562) representing the two largest categories. CAs self-report only 31% of incidents, while external researchers discover 17%, automated tools find 15%, and root programs identify just 4%. Policy failures account for 238 incidents and disclosure failures for 159, indicating that CAs struggle both to follow requirements and to transparently report when they fail, a pattern that directly undermines the audit oversight measured in the audit intelligence analysis.
intros.crypto: The cryptographic posture analysis examines root certificate algorithms, key sizes, and compliance with modern standards across the 335 roots in the trust surface. Migration from SHA-1 to SHA-256 signing and from 2048-bit to 4096-bit RSA keys has progressed unevenly, with legacy roots persisting in some trust stores years after algorithm deprecation timelines. ECDSA P-256 and P-384 roots have grown in prevalence but remain a minority of the installed base, while post-quantum preparation remains in early research phases with no production deployment timeline.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have been recorded, with compliance and operational failure driving 14 cases and a pattern of repeated issues triggering 10 events. Negligent noncompliance accounts for 7 distrust postures, demonstrated incompetence for 3, and willful circumvention for 3, while only 1 case was classified as accidental. The median runway from distrust announcement to root removal is 1,185 days (over three years), reflecting browsers' cautious approach to minimize ecosystem disruption even when facing CAs that have exhibitedArgumentative noncompliance or repeated governance failures.
intros.policy: Among 43 active TLS-issuing CAs measured for SC-081 compliance, 3 remain at risk of missing the March 2026 200-day validity deadline and 5 have not yet met the March 2027 100-day threshold based on observed certificate replacement behavior. The median current validity period is 62 days, indicating many CAs have already adopted the March 2029 47-day target, though 9 have formally demonstrated readiness while others lag. This uneven readiness occurs against a compliance surface that has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations (76% mandatory), with no new CA/B Forum ballots passed since 2022 even as operational complexity continues to increase.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 68% (Chrome) and 78% (Mozilla) of incidents in 2019 to just 18% (Chrome) and 10% (Mozilla) in 2025, with Apple at 5% and Microsoft at 0%. Chrome has filed substantive comments on 296 of 740 oversight bugs, Mozilla on 250 of 821, and Apple on just 6 of 46, while Microsoft participates in zero public incident discussions. This decline in active governance occurs as the incident rate remains high (223 bugs in 2025 vs 255 in 2019), leaving the majority of CA compliance failures to self-reporting and external researchers rather than program-led enforcement.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 21 participate actively, leaving 35 with zero ballot contributions or discussion engagement. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo leads individual participation with 36 ballots proposed and 1 endorsed, while Sectigo is the most active organizational contributor overall. This concentration of ecosystem governance work among a small subset of members means policy development depends on a narrow group of voices, many representing high-volume CAs whose commercial interests may not align with the tail operators or relying party community.
intros.audit: Auditors detected only 30% of incidents that occurred during the audit period they reviewed, meaning 70% of the 427 in-scope compliance failures went unreported in audit letters that subsequently declared unqualified opinions. 41 CAs show high transparency gaps between clean audit findings and actual incident histories, while only 5 audit letters carry qualified opinions despite widespread governance and misissuance problems. 62.9% of WebTrust and 69.7% of ETSI audit findings come from CA self-reports rather than auditor-initiated discovery, indicating that audit letters function more as compliance theater than independent surveillance of the operational risk documented across 1,743 total incidents.
